docs.title: 8.1 96×64 pixel OLED display (0xFFFF0020–0xFFFF002C)
docs.text:
• Resolution: 96 Columns $\times$ 64 Rows ($288\text{px} \times 192\text{px}$ canvas at 3x scale).
  • Color Formats (OLED_CTRL[7:4]):
  • 0x0: 8-bit Color (3-Red, 3-Green, 2-Blue)
  • 0x1: 16-bit Color (5-Red, 6-Green, 5-Blue / RGB565)
  • 0x2: 24-bit RGB Color (8-Red, 8-Green, 8-Blue)
  • Advance Modes (OLED_CTRL[3:0]):
  • 0x0 (vary_pixel_data_mode): Writing OLED_DATA updates the current pixel without modifying coordinates.
  • 0x1 (vary_col_mode): Writing OLED_DATA updates pixel and increments column index (col = (col + 1) % 96).
  • 0x2 (vary_row_mode): Writing OLED_DATA updates pixel and increments row index (row = (row + 1) % 64).
  • 0x4 (autoadvance_col): Column auto-advances across line; wraps to next row when reaching column 95.
  • 0x5 (autoadvance_row): Row auto-advances down column; wraps to next column when reaching row 63. Perfect for column-major framebuffer streams.

docs.title: 8.2 3-axis accelerometer & temperature sensor (0xFFFF0040–0xFFFF0044)
docs.text:
• 0xFFFF0040 (RO): ACCEL_DATA — 32-bit packed {temperature, X, Y, Z} from MSB to LSB:
  • [31:24]: Temperature (8-bit signed integer, $-40..+85^\circ\text{C}$, default 25 / 0x19, offset +3).
  • [23:16]: X Acceleration (8-bit signed integer, $\pm 2g$, default 0 / 0x00 = $0.00g$, offset +2).
  • [15:8]: Y Acceleration (8-bit signed integer, $\pm 2g$, default 0 / 0x00 = $0.00g$, offset +1).
  • [7:0]: Z Acceleration (8-bit signed integer, $\pm 2g$, default +64 / 0x40 = $+1.00g$, offset +0).
  • 0xFFFF0044 (RO): ACCEL_DREADY — Bit 0 = 1 when data is ready.
  • Interactive Controls & Presets: Range sliders for X, Y, Z ($\pm 128$), temperature slider, live $g$-force calculation, and presets (Flat, Tilt X ±1g, Tilt Y ±1g, Shake ±2g, Zero All). The Tilt X / Tilt Y presets are toggles: the first click sets the axis to $-1g$ (X or Y to -64/0xC0, Z to 0), and the second click flips to +1g (+64), repeating alternately.

docs.title: 8.3 UART serial console (0xFFFF0000–0xFFFF000C)
docs.text:
• Memory-mapped serial terminal with independent output buffer, auto-sequencer delay, hex/ASCII I/O modes, and responsive flex wrapping.
  • ASCII mode: Type raw text (including escapes such as \r, \n, \t, \xHH); the terminal echoes the raw characters as they are transmitted.
  • Hex mode: Type comma-separated hex bytes — each token is interpreted as a hex byte with or without the 0x/0X prefix (e.g. 0x48, 0x69, 0x0D or 48, 69, 0D; a single trailing h suffix such as 69h is also accepted). Tokens larger than 0xFF or non-hex tokens are silently skipped. The terminal output re-renders live as 0xHH bytes (e.g. 0x41 0x0D) and stays in hex view across program-run batches, steppers, and resets — switching the mode back to ASCII re-renders the same transmitted bytes as raw text.
  • Mobile-friendly input: the transmit field uses autocomplete="off", autocapitalize="off", spellcheck="false", and enterkeyhint="send", and the global keyboard shortcuts (F5/F8/F9/Ctrl+Enter/Ctrl+S) are suppressed while any form field is focused, so the on-screen keyboard stays open and typing is not interrupted.

docs.title: 9. Pre-loaded example programs
docs.text:
The simulator comes pre-loaded with 13 rich example programs (7 in Assembly and 6 in C). dip_led / dip_led_c are the two baked into the page; every other example is fetched from examples/asm/ or examples/c/ when selected, which is what needs the page served over http:// (see the file table at the top of this document).

The menu itself is not hardcoded either. examples/index.txt (plain text, not .md — a static site generator hosting this repo tends to render .md through its own Markdown pipeline rather than serve it verbatim, which broke this fetch) each hold one markdown-style table — | key | label | file | description | per row — parsed at startup into the dropdown and the file each key maps to. Adding a program is a row in the matching index plus the .asm/.c file itself; nothing in riscv_simulator.html changes. Both tables are designed for up to 15 rows; nothing enforces that as a hard limit, it is just what the dropdown's layout assumes. Until that fetch resolves — permanently, over file://, where it never will — the menu falls back to the one baked example in each language, so it is never genuinely empty.

docs.title: 9.1 C examples (6)
docs.text:
1. dip_led_c (DIP to LED): C translation of DIP_to_LED.asm — mirrors the DIP switches onto the LEDs on a short polling delay. The one C example baked into the page.
  2. fibonacci_c (Fibonacci): Iterative Fibonacci series generator storing values in an array.
  3. hello_world_c (Hello World): C translation of HelloWorld.asm — a single unstructured-but-goto-free loop with one state variable, no callee function, matching how HelloWorld.asm predates jal/jalr in the course.
  4. hello_jal_c (Hello Subroutine): C translation of HelloWorld_jal_jalr.asm — the same echo loop, but the greeting is printed by a real function, print_string(const char *s), taking the string as a parameter the way PRINT_S takes it in a0.
  5. circle_accel_c (Circle & Delay Accel - Circle_delay_accel.c): Implements the Midpoint Circle Algorithm on the OLED display, polls accelerometer X/Y tilt, animates circle positions, outputs frame counts to the 7-Segment display, and sends UART telemetry.
  6. image_display_c (Image Display & Accel - ImageDisplay_autoadvance_accel.c): High-performance OLED graphics rendering using Auto-Advance Mode 5 (autoadvance_row), displaying 96x64 8-bit color bitmap artwork (Uphill.png / Downhill.png), responding dynamically to X-axis accelerometer tilt, and logging status messages to the UART terminal.

docs.title: 9.2 Assembly examples (7)
docs.text:
1. dip_led (DIP_to_LED.asm): Direct hardware loop copying 16-bit DIP switch states directly to output LEDs. The one example baked into the page.
  2. rars_syscalls (rars_syscalls.asm): Comprehensive demonstration of RARS ecall services (print string, integer, hex, char, exit).
  3. fib (fibonacci.asm): Computes Fibonacci numbers in registers x1–x5.
  4. hello_world (HelloWorld.asm): Direct character-by-character UART transmission of "Hello World".
  5. hello_jal (HelloWorld_jal_jalr.asm): Modular UART printing subroutine utilizing jal and jalr.
  6. circle_accel (Circle_delay_accel.asm): Complete assembly implementation of OLED circle rendering and accelerometer integration.
  7. image_display_accel (ImageDisplay_autoadvance_accel.asm): Assembly implementation of 96x64 image display using auto-advance mode 5 and accelerometer tilt detection.

The DIP_to_LED and HelloWorld assembly examples double as the HDL mode's smoke tests — they exercise a DIP read, an LED write and the full UART handshake against real RTL in a few hundred cycles.

docs.title: 10. Processor state, ISA reference & RARS syscalls
10.1 Register bank structure
docs.text:
Models 32 32-bit integer registers (x0–x31), 32 floating-point registers (f0–f31), and the Program Counter (PC). Register x0 is hardwired to 0x00000000. - Hardware-Accurate Stack Pointer: sp (register x2) is initialized to 0x00000000 on reset as per RISC-V hardware specification.

+-----+----------+-------------------+-------------------+
|  #  | ABI Name |   Content (Hex)   |   Content (Dec)   |
+-----+----------+-------------------+-------------------+
| x0  |   zero   |     00000000      |         0         |
| x1  |    ra    |     00010040      |       65600       |
| x2  |    sp    |     00000000      |         0         |
| ... |   ...    |        ...        |        ...        |
+-----+----------+-------------------+-------------------+
No 0x prefix on Content (Hex) — the header already says it's hex; Memory's Addr column is the one place that keeps 0x, since its header doesn't.

docs.title: 12. Automated test suite
docs.text:
A Node/jsdom harness lives in riscv_simulator_tests/. Every suite loads the real riscv_simulator.html, so the tests exercise the shipped file rather than a copy of its logic. npm test runs all 18 of them — every test_*.js file in the directory is one of the 18, there is no build step and nothing else to run. The remaining files there are shared test infrastructure, not suites of their own: godbolt_cache.js/.json mock Godbolt's response for C compilation, and examples_fetch.js serves examples/ from disk — both stand in for network access jsdom does not have.

Test script Target subsystem & scenarios test_comprehensive_suite.js Full system integration: editor proxy facade, Tab precision, breakpoints, assembler, stepping, history undo, FPGA MMIO registers, toolbar layout, and (sections [11]–[12]) every finding of the assembler audit — operand arity, range checks, label rules, register naming in the disassembly, the PC readout and the ecall notice. test_hdl_mode.js HDL mode, end to end (159 assertions). Drives the real Icarus/WASM pipeline over the unmodified RV/*.v sources — see below. test_panel_grid.js Dockable-panel 2×2 grid layout, splitters, per-panel column sizing and persistence. test_c_godbolt_simulation.js Godbolt REST API compilation, bidirectional line mapping, C breakpoints and C stepping. test_new_c_simulation.js Compilation and execution of Circle_delay_accel.c and ImageDisplay_autoadvance_accel.c. test_baked_examples_full.js Compilation and execution of the four heaviest built-in examples, two in assembly and two in C. test_statement_stepping.js Statement Stepping in both C and ASM, multi-instruction execution and discrete step back. test_sim_max_instructions_setting.js Run-limit setting and execution-loop throttling. test_disassembly_labels_and_warnings.js Label header rendering, jump/branch target annotations, FPGA hardware notice. test_disassembly_machine_code.js Machine-code Byte/Word modes and binary byte grouping. test_reset_and_image_display.js OLED auto-advance mode 5 rendering fidelity, ASM/C pixel parity, peripheral reset. test_tab_and_autocomplete.js CM6 key handling, literal Tab insertion, block indent, operand autocomplete, signature help. test_breakpoint_highlight_and_snap.js Breakpoint snapping from comments/blanks/directives, gutter highlight pill. test_all_instructions_v2.js RV32GC translation coverage across 90+ instructions and pseudo-ops — that they assemble. test_instruction_semantics.js That they are right (136 cases). Each instruction is executed and its result checked against a value worked out from the spec, exercising encoder → machine code → decoder → execution. Mutation-tested against 12 seeded faults. test_execution_programs.js Multi-step execution and register assertions for Factorial ($5! = 120$) and Fibonacci ($F_9=34$, $F_{10}=55$). test_mobile_keyboard_focus.js On-screen-keyboard focus preservation across panel relayout. test_m_extension.js RV32M, three ways (21 assertions). All eight M instructions over six operand pairs, on the JS engine, on RV/*.v through Icarus, and against a BigInt reference; plus the stall, and the pre-synthesised examples/hdl/RV_reference.v. test_jsdom.js Boot smoke test under jsdom.

docs.title: 12.1 Instruction semantics, and why assembling is not enough
docs.text:
test_all_instructions_v2.js proves a long program containing every instruction assembles with no errors. That catches a mnemonic falling out of the table — it does not catch a wrong funct7, a decoder that sign-extends where it should not, or a pseudo-instruction whose expansion has drifted. Each of those produces a program that assembles cleanly and computes the wrong answer.

test_instruction_semantics.js runs each instruction and checks the result. Because the encoder and the interpreter are separate code paths, that one check exercises encoder → machine code → decoder → execution, and a mistake in either end shows up as a wrong number. Expected values come from the RISC-V spec, not from the simulator: a check that agrees with the implementation by construction tests nothing.

The suite is mutation-tested — its own coverage is measured by seeding faults into the simulator and confirming each is caught:

Seeded fault Caught SRAI made a logical shift 2 cases SLTI < made <= 1 SLTIU < made <= 1 BGE >= made > 5 SUB encoded with ADD's funct7 6 XORI encoded as ORI 1 BLTU encoded as BLT 2 LHU sign-extending 1 mv, neg, snez, sgtz, seqz expansions corrupted 1–2 each

Two of those initially slipped through — SLTI and seqz — both because no case sat on the boundary that distinguishes the correct behaviour from the faulty one. Cases were added until all twelve were caught, which is why the suite carries a deliberate boundary case for every comparison: equal as well as less and greater, zero as well as positive and negative.

docs.title: 12.2 The HDL suite
docs.text:
test_hdl_mode.js is the one that needs real tooling: it loads the page, assembles through the normal assembler, asks the page for the artefacts it would hand to Icarus (the generic testbench, the memory images, the stimulus files), then runs the real Icarus pipeline over the unmodified RV/*.v sources.

  • Discovery finds dut.RV1.RegFile1.RegBank, and still finds it after the module, the instance and the array are all renamed.
  • The testbench is program-independent: byte-identical Verilog for two different programs with different switch settings, and no DIP value anywhere in it.
  • One compile, many runs: the same binary gives LED=0xad for +DIP=bead and LED=0x72 for +DIP=0072, and runs standalone with no plusargs at all.
  • The trace starts at the reset vector, never reports a write to x0, captures the DIP value landing in a register and the store to the LED MMIO address.
  • Stepping reaches the right state either side of the instruction that reads the DIP switches, and stepping back undoes the register write.
  • A mid-run input change takes effect (0xad → 0xff) while the history before it stays bit-identical — the property the whole interaction model rests on.
  • MMIO timing, both directions: an input changed while paused is read by the very next instruction (not the one after it), and the LED shows its new value as soon as the storing instruction completes.
  • Breakpoints: Resume stops on the breakpoint line, resumes to the next time that line is reached, and runs to the end of the recording when there are none.
  • RX_VALID: both bytes are acknowledged, the FIFO empties on the instruction that reads each one, and stepping back puts the byte back.
  • Statement Stepping in HDL: with it off a Step is one machine instruction; with it on a Step covers the whole source line, and Back undoes exactly that.
  • HelloWorld: 'A' + CR delivered through uart_rx.mem produces the echo and the greeting stored in DMEM, exercising UART_RX/valid/ack and UART_TX/valid.
node riscv_simulator_tests/test_hdl_mode.js

The engine is expected at the path in HDL_ENGINE_DIR; point it at a folder holding the six engine files to run the full pipeline offline. Node 20+ is required — the Emscripten modules are ES modules using import.meta.

All 15 suites above pass against riscv_simulator.html.

docs.title: 13. Version history
docs.text:
Newest first. Versions before v15.0 are grouped.

Version Milestone description & features implemented v24.113 (One Simulation Tab) Settings has three tabs: Compiler, Linker and ⏱ Simulation, which replaces JS Simulation and HDL Simulation. It opens with what reaches both engines (Statement Stepping, the clock), each now a single control instead of a copy on each tab kept in step; below that, the active engine's settings only (#simGroupJs or #simGroupHdl, hidden by refreshSimSettingsScope), where the JS group used to be dimmed with a note in HDL mode. Switching to HDL with no sources opens this tab, which then shows them. Reset Defaults on it resets the active engine's settings. Messages that pointed at "Settings > HDL" now say Settings > Simulation. v24.112 (A Clock, and Real Time) The clock. ⚙ Settings (both tabs, kept in step) takes CLK_DIV_BITS as TOP_Nexys.vhd does: the CPU clock is 100 MHz ÷ 2^(N+1), or 100 MHz at 0 (cpuHz). The stats bar shows the simulated time of the cycles so far beside the count. The UART's Paste gap is now derived from it, one character at 115200 baud being 8640 clocks of uart.vhd's 100 MHz (uartCharCycles: 135 at the default 5), and the box shows it read-only; Typed is still set by hand. UART delivery now counts clock cycles in every model (uartNow returns totalCycles), which in single-cycle is the same as instructions and in multi-cycle is now correct. Real time (the Run choice beside the clock; Max speed, the old behaviour, is the default). The JS run loop runs, each tick, the cycles the clock has owed since the run began, using the model's own cycle count, and waits for the next one; a tick works for at most 30 ms so the page keeps redrawing. More than a quarter second behind, the debt is dropped and the reached fraction shows in the stats bar (×0.14 real time). Measured: single-cycle holds 99.7% at 12.5 MHz, the pipeline 99.4% at 1.56 MHz, and 100 MHz reaches about a tenth. Below 1 kHz each tick also redraws the registers and the current line, so execution can be watched. HDL playback. vvp cannot be paced, so a run is recorded as before and then played back (hdlPlayTo): every frame seeks to the last instruction that has begun by now at the clock, and Run becomes Pause meanwhile; Step, Back, a new run or an input change stop it, and the run's summary and status are given when it ends. Measured against the reference core at 6.1 kHz: 2,000 cycles in 328 ms. The stats bar reads time, then cycles, then instructions. v24.111 (Credit to Harris & Harris) Credits names Sarah L. Harris and David Harris, Digital Design and Computer Architecture: RISC-V Edition, for the microarchitecture terminology and some general ideas, and says the datapaths here are a different design from the book's. v24.110 (Single-Cycle Steps Named by Pipeline Stage; a Clock Beside the Drawing) The nine single-cycle steps follow the pipeline's stages, so the two microarchitectures read as one story: Fetch; Decode · Decoder (the field fan-out and the Decoder's outputs, previously two steps), Decode · Register Read, Decode · Extend (split from register read); Execute · ALU and PC Logic (PC Logic's PCSrc moves here from the old Next PC step); Memory; Writeback · Register Write, Writeback · PC Increment (the target adder and its muxes), Writeback · Retire (the clock edge). Each phase carries a stage, and the header shows the stage name in the pipeline's colour for it (on a phone only the step name; the clock shows the stage). The clock: the single-cycle drawing's viewBox is widened 320 units to the left (dpClockInit, which reads the viewBox attribute rather than viewBox.baseVal, which jsdom lacks) and one clock period is drawn there: CLK, a rising edge at the top, high for the first half, low for the second, and the next rising edge at the bottom; beside it the nine steps as boxes in their stage colours, the current one solid, those done half-tinted (dpClockUpdate). At Retire the bottom edge is lit amber: the transition to the next instruction. Being part of the drawing, it scales with it and costs no height. The "Press ▶ to let the edge happen" sentence is gone from Retire's caption. v24.109 (Arrows Walk the Single-Cycle Phases; a Caption That Keeps Its Height) With the single-cycle datapath on screen, → and ← move a phase, as the strip's ▶ and ◀ do, and → past the clock edge executes and moves to the next instruction as before; without it, or pipelined, they Step and Back. ◀ (and ←) at the first phase now goes back to the instruction before, at its last phase, instead of doing nothing, and is enabled whenever there is history. On desktop the caption keeps its height when empty: collapsing it at phase 0 gave the drawing its space, so the diagram zoomed in at each new instruction and back out at the next phase. On a phone, where the drawing scales by width, an empty caption still takes no space. v24.108 (One Meaning per Key: Arrows Step, J K L Press, , . Nudge) → and ← are Step and Back (F8, Shift+F8), outside the editor and form fields. The push buttons, held for a momentary press, move from ← ↓ → to J K L, left to right as BTNL, BTNC, BTNR; the accelerometer nudge, hold X/Y/Z/T, moves from ← → to , and ., which sit left and right of each other as the sliders move. A first cut kept the arrows as push buttons while running and made them step only when paused, which gave one key two meanings. Stepping is deliberately not mentioned in the UI or the guide; the push-button and accelerometer hints and tooltips name their new keys, and the arrow under each push button is gone. The letters work with Shift or Caps Lock too (< and > count as , and .). v24.107 (A Cross-Check for Any Microarchitecture; Statement Stepping in the Pipeline) The cross-check (hdlCompareWithJs) stepped the functional model in lockstep with the hardware trace by PC and compared registers after each step. The trace records one step per change of the Wrapper's PC, which is the instruction completing in a single-cycle core but the fetch PC in a pipeline, so any correct pipelined core failed: at the first taken branch, whose wrong-path fetches look like a PC divergence, or at the first register rewritten, since its write lands several steps after its fetch. It now compares effects: the sequence of register changes and the sequence of data-memory byte writes, the hardware's taken from the trace's @@W and @@M records (which now keep their own cycle) and the model's from lastExecutedRd and a writeMem wrapper during a replay from reset with the run's starting inputs. Both sides treat registers as starting at 0, as the hardware's do, so a first write of 0 is no change on either. The first difference is reported with its cycle, both values, and the instruction and source line that produced the model's; if an input changed during the run, the comparison stops at that cycle. test_hdl_mode.js [8a] passes a real single-cycle run, the same run rewritten as a pipeline would record it (every register write four fetches late, wrong-path fetches between), and reports a corrupted value at its own cycle. A pipelined core is noticed after a run (hdlLooksPipelined: most register writes land in a step whose instruction has a different rd), and the console says that Step, Back, breakpoints and the instruction count follow the fetch PC. Statement Stepping now works pipelined: a Step clocks until the statement's last instruction has left Write-back (pipeStatementStep). The statement is the oldest instruction's, and only W, M and E are consulted after that, since D and F may yet be flushed; a breakpoint entering Execute also stops it. The strip's ▶ still clocks one cycle. v24.106 (The Strip's ⚙ Opens Settings; Settings Work From the Start) The JS model's Settings controls (the microarchitecture select, the hazard switches, branch prediction) got their onchange handlers from pipeInitControls, which only ran when the Settings dialog was first built. Until then they changed nothing: ticking branch prediction in the strip's popover before ever opening Settings showed a tick that did not reach pipeBP, and the next step ran without it. initDatapath now wires them at load. The popover, which moved the Settings card's switches into itself and back, is gone; the ⚙ beside Pipelined opens Settings on JS Simulation, scrolled to the Microarchitecture card (openPipeSettings). On desktop the strip's controls stay right-aligned in pipelined mode: the rule that starts them at the left when the instruction slot is empty is now phone-only. v24.105 (The Saved Testbench Replays the Run; Only the Chosen Model's Settings) Download → Testbench used to save the generic testbench, which reads the program-independent run settings as plusargs and the recorded inputs from stim.mem and uart_rx.mem; a student got none of those, so the saved file could not reproduce what the page had shown. hdlBuildTestbench({ run }) now bakes one run in as the defaults: the cycle budget, the switch, button and accelerometer values at cycle 0, and every timed input change and UART byte, written into stim_mem and rx_mem by an initial block, with the header saying what it replays and that AA_IROM.mem and AA_DMEM.mem go beside it. The plusargs still override, and the page's own runs still use the generic form with everything supplied at run time. Saved in JS mode or before any HDL run, it starts from the inputs as they are, with no timeline (hdlCurrentInputs, which leaves the recorded run's base alone). test_hdl_mode.js [7b] compiles such a testbench, runs it with only the two program images and no plusargs, and checks that the LEDs show the starting switches and then the mid-run change, identically to the same run through the generic testbench and a stimulus file. Also, the JS model's settings show only what the chosen microarchitecture uses (the hazard and prediction switches for the pipeline, the cycle table for multi-cycle, neither for single-cycle) instead of dimming the rest; the cycle table sits inside the Microarchitecture card, as the pipeline's switches do. v24.104 (Single-Cycle, Multi-Cycle or Pipelined) The JS model's Microarchitecture is a three-way choice. "Single-cycle" used to take its cycle count from the per-category table, which is a multi-cycle model under the wrong name; it now counts one cycle per instruction, Multi-cycle is the table (moved up to sit under the choice, and dimmed otherwise), and the pipeline counts clock edges as before. jsArch holds the choice; pipeMode is kept as jsArch === 'pipe' for the pipeline code, and pipeSetMode is a wrapper over setJsArch. Switching between any two resets the program, since the count so far belongs to the other model. The stats bar tags the count single, multi, pipe or hw, with CPI for multi-cycle as well as pipelined. Multi-cycle has no drawing, so it blocks the Datapath button as an undrawable program does, with its own tooltip; the strip's dropdown still offers only Single-cycle and Pipelined. Also: the Linker tab's "FPGA Hardware Notice:" label is gone, leaving its one line. v24.103 (Phone: No Panel Headers; the Floating Steps Fixed) On a phone only one panel shows at a time and the lit tab names it, so panel headers are hidden there; the filter they carried, for Registers, Memory, Disassembly and Locals, is a 🔍 at the right end of the tab strip, outside its scrolling part, acting on the current tab (updateMobileFindBtn, refreshed by applyPanelDock). Desktop keeps its headers, since panels stack and float there. The floating step buttons never appeared on a real phone: floatOnDpTab tested body.dp-open, which is the desktop strip's state, not the phone panel's (browser checks had passed only because that session had once opened the desktop strip). It now tests the datapath panel's visibility, so the header drops its own ◀ ▶ ▶▶ and fits; its empty instruction and phase slots take no space and the controls start at the left. The phone timeline is as tall as its rows instead of the diagram's 300 px minimum. v24.102 (BranchPred.svg Redrawn Again; the Branch Predictor Opens) The v24.97 drawing used the pipelined drawing's shapes but not its conventions: labels in several sizes and weights, explanatory text and equations on the canvas, and every E-side signal gathered into a bundle off the BHT's right edge, run across to gates in the far corner. tools/bp_figure.py now lays it out as Microarch_pipelined.svg is drawn: every wire label 37 regular, placed on the wire at the block it leaves or enters, control and its labels blue, only block names 46 bold, no prose; PC Logic as that drawing's two-line rotated block; the stalls, flushes and Mispredict running down to a Hazard Unit bar. The BHT sits below Execute, so its second port takes PCE, PCSrcE and PCNextE from directly above, the misprediction check (XOR, ≠, AND, OR) is beside it, and the two write enables enter from below; only port 1, the index from PCF and the prediction back to Fetch, runs the width of the drawing, as the lecture drawing's rdE and ResultW do. In the simulator, clicking the pipelined diagram's Branch Predictor block (pointer and tooltip on hover) opens this drawing in a dialog, embedded by tools/bp_figure.py --embed so it works offline; Escape or ✕ closes it. v24.101 (A One-Row Datapath Header; Captions Below the Drawing) On a phone the single-cycle strip spent three rows above the drawing: the instruction with "ready · 9 phases", the dropdowns wrapped below it, and a caption telling the user to press ▶ or ▶▶. The idle status and the hint are gone, and an empty caption takes no space. While stepping, the header shows the phase ("2/9 Decode") on the same row as the instruction and the dropdowns: on a phone the header no longer wraps, its type is a size smaller, the instruction drops its address and gives way with an ellipsis. The caption, single-cycle and pipelined, is now below the drawing (order: 1 in the strip's column), so nothing sits between the instruction and its picture. v24.100 (A Timeline That Fits Across) The timeline no longer scrolls sideways. pdpRenderTimeline builds the chart with up to 18 cycles, measures it, and rebuilds it with only as many as fit the strip's width, working from the label column's width and the per-cycle width it just measured; at a 500 px strip that is 7 cycles, at 700 px 15. On a phone it shows only the rows in flight (the up to five instructions and any bubbles), starting at the cycle the oldest of them entered, with no addresses in the labels, which alone would have taken the width of several cycles. v24.99 (Floating Step Buttons on a Phone; Bubbles in the Timeline) Step buttons float on a phone (#floatSteps, updateFloatSteps): a small pill of 36 px buttons at the bottom right, below dialogs in the stacking order. On the Datapath tab it is always there and is the strip's ◀ ▶ ▶▶ (body.float-dp hides the header's own copies, which is also what lets the pipelined header fit a phone's width: with them it was 453 px in a 368 px strip, ▶▶ and the speed clipped). Elsewhere it appears once the toolbar's Step is less than 60% on screen (an IntersectionObserver): the strip's controls when pipelined, where they step cycles, otherwise the toolbar's Back and Step, which covers HDL mode and its waveform. It mirrors the source buttons' enabled state from updateToolbarButtonStates, the HDL override included, so an asynchronous HDL step re-enables it. Stepping also stopped dragging a scrolled phone page back to the top: the executing line was centred with CodeMirror's scrollIntoView effect, which scrolls every scrollable ancestor, the window included, whenever the line is outside the editor's view; centreEditorLine now scrolls the editor alone. Disassembly's follow-the-PC scroll likewise moves only its panel body, allowing for the sticky header, and now also runs on the phone tab, which its docked-or-floating test had left out. The cycle count. The pipelined strip header no longer shows its own count, which crowded the phone header and read one ahead of the log (the header gave the cycle about to be clocked, the log the one just clocked); the timeline's live column is headed next rather than numbered, for the same reason. Bubbles in the timeline. A stage left empty used to show as nothing, so a stall or a flush looked like four instructions in flight. pdpRenderTimeline now works out each bubble from consecutive columns: an empty stage whose predecessor stage held an instruction the cycle before is a nop of its own if that instruction is still there (a stall, or a serial instruction's drain), and that instruction, quashed, if it is gone; a bubble then moves on a stage a cycle. The nop gets a row, "bubble (nop)", between the instructions it separates; a quashed instruction's row goes on, labelled "→ bubble (nop)", its later cells dashed. A serial instruction leaving D by executing, and the pipeline filling or running dry, are just empty. The trace gains a serial flag for that, and the chart looks four cycles behind its window so a bubble already in flight at the left edge still has its row. GoatCounter's site code is set (cg3207sim). v24.98 (Pipeline Controls in the Strip; Phone Layout; Feedback) The strip's view toggle, a lone "Timeline" button that was easy to miss, is a Diagram v24.97 (BranchPred.svg Redrawn as Vector) The course's BranchPred.svg was a PNG wrapped in an SVG. It is now drawn by tools/bp_figure.py as plain vector shapes and text, in the style of Microarch_pipelined.svg (data black, control blue, and that drawing's mux, adder, register, clock and memory shapes, line weights and fonts), with the original's level of detail (the BHT as a table; the check at gate level with the XOR, the comparator, the AND and the OR), but as the simulator implements it: the target and the recovery PC are both PCNextE from the next-PC adder, (PCE or RD1FwdE) + ExtImmE or PCE + 4, so jalr is covered and the figure's correction mux and the PCPlus4 and predicted target carried through D and E are gone; the BHT's second port reads and writes at PCE; each PrPCSrc is one bit or a 2-bit counter; and Mispredict selects the PC and drives FlushD and FlushE. v24.96 (Branch Prediction for the Pipeline) An option of the pipelined microarchitecture, off by default, set in Settings with a 1-bit or 2-bit predictor and 4 to 256 entries; changing any of it resets the program. A BHT indexed by PC[k+1:2], untagged, read in F before decode, so every instruction is predicted (pipeBhtIndex, pipeBhtTaken): each entry holds a predicted PCSrc (one bit, or a saturating counter whose top bit is the prediction) and a predicted target. F fetches PrBTAF when PrPCSrcF, else PCF + 4. The next-PC adder's result for the instruction in E, PCNextE (its target if PCSrcE, else PCE + 4), is both the recovery PC and what the predicted target is checked against: Branch Mispredicted = PrPCSrcE xor PCSrcE, BTA Mispredicted = PCSrcE and PrBTAE != BTAE, and either flushes D and E (the flush switch reads "Flush on misprediction") and loads PCNextE. The 1-bit entry is written on a branch misprediction and the target on a BTA misprediction, as in the course's BranchPred figure; the 2-bit counter steps on every instruction in E, which is what "every instruction is predicted" makes of a counter. Unlike the figure, the prediction is not carried through D and E: a second read port at PCE gives E the same entry F saw, since the table only changes when that instruction mispredicts (flushing everything younger) or, for a counter, by a step that cannot flip its top bit. A serial instruction (FP, ecall) executes in D and never reaches E, so with prediction on it always redirects to its own next PC, dropping a fetch that may have followed a wrong prediction made for it. The BHT is copied whole into each Step's snapshot. Fields that are genuinely unsigned get no signed reading at all, because they have none: slli x11, x5, -1, lui x9, -0x1 and auipc x10, -1 are all rejected, so a shift amount reads 0..31 and a lui immediate 0..1048575, each with a hex spelling and, for U-type, the value it actually loads or adds (0xfffff000). Branch and jump targets give the resolved address and the distance, and keep their <label> badge. The field is decoded from the encoded word rather than from the source token, so a value written in hex, the same value written in decimal and one a pseudo-op computed all read alike. And .editor-container textarea survived the move to CodeMirror as a dangling selector glued to the next rule: written as .editor-container textarea, immediately above /* Toolbar */ .toolbar {, it silently gave that phantom element every toolbar style, with a second copy grouped onto .console in the mobile block. Harmless only because no such element exists. Both removed. The Settings compatibility shims kept their comment's claim that applyMemSegments and resetMemSegments are "exercised by riscv_simulator_tests" - they are not, and nothing in the page calls the six of them either, so the comment now says that instead of inventing a dependency. Also checked and clean: no duplicate element ids, no var, and all fifteen loose-equality uses are == null or text inside doc strings. v24.74 (UART Receive Models the Hardware: One Byte, Paced Arrival, and Overrun) The console held received bytes in an unbounded array, so a polling loop that could not keep up simply accumulated characters and looked correct - while the board, which has one holding register and no FIFO anywhere (uart.vhd buffers nothing; the single byte lives in TOP_Nexys.vhd:455-471), discards the newer character, keeps the older, and raises no flag. HDL mode was lossless too, by a different route: the generated testbench held a byte until UART_RX_ack before offering the next, which is back-pressure a wire cannot apply. The receive path is now two-sided, as the real one is: uartPending is the PC's transmit buffer, and uartRxByte/uartRxFull is the FPGA's single register. Delivery is paced - one character is 8640 clocks at 115200 baud, which is 135 instructions at the default CLK_DIV_BITS - and a byte arriving while the register is full is dropped, oldest kept, counted, and reported in the console with the reason. Pacing is not separable from the register depth: with instant delivery a one-deep register would keep only the first byte of any send, so the two had to land together, and the reframing is what makes it coherent - the queue is the PC clocking bytes out at baud rate, not a receive FIFO. The Buffer checkbox and its instruction-delay box are replaced by an Arrival select: Paste (baud rate, the default), Typed (human speed), Forgiving (waits for the program, never drops - not what the board does, kept for debugging logic rather than timing). An Instant option was considered and rejected: against a one-deep register it would deliver one byte and drop the rest, which is not an escape hatch but a trap. The testbench's RX feed now mirrors TOP_Nexys - arrival on timestamp, discard on overrun - and hdlSyncRx() stamps pending bytes a character apart instead of all at cycle 0, so the two engines agree. Two Wrapper.v fixes went with it, both local to RV/: the read mux returned ACCEL_DReady for a read of UART_RX with nothing waiting, now a defined 0; and UART_RX_ack could stay high across two back-to-back loads, which TOP edge-detects on the faster clock as a single ack, leaving the second load's result dependent on when TOP got round to clearing valid. Adding && !UART_RX_ack gives every load that sees valid its own edge. That last one was going to be modelled in the simulator until it became clear it is a race rather than a behaviour - modelling it would have presented timing-dependence as determinism - so it was fixed instead, and the simulator needs nothing for it. test_hdl_mode.js [10] and [13] fed two bytes at cycle: 0 and relied on the old back-pressure; they now space them realistically, which is the point of the change rather than a casualty. v24.73 (OLED Swap Status as a Badge; OLED_STATUS_OFF in the Examples) The Peripherals panel showed OLED_STATUS as a 32-bit hex row, which read as data rather than as the status flag it is. Replaced with a SWAP PENDING: 0 badge in the section title, matching how DREADY, RX VALID and TX READY are already presented. The buffering line below it stays, and is the more informative of the two in the simulator: the badge is always 0 because no scanout is modelled, whereas the page state changes as a program presents. OLED_STATUS_OFF 0x30 was added to the offset block of every example that carries one - four C files and three assembly files. Circle_delay_accel.asm and ImageDisplay_autoadvance_accel.asm are raw compiler output with no .eqv block and fibonacci/rars_syscalls have no MMIO block at all, so they were left alone. DIP_to_LED.c is also embedded in riscv_simulator.html as the baked example, and the two copies must stay byte-identical or installGodboltCache() stops matching and the suites fall through to the live API; both were changed together and all six C examples were confirmed to still hit the cache. An unused #define generates no code, so the cached assembly stays valid. v24.72 (OLED Swap Status Moves to Its Own Register, OLED_STATUS) v24.70 read the swap-pending flag back through OLED_CTRL, which made one address mean two unrelated things depending on direction. Split out to OLED_STATUS at 0xFFFF0030, read-only, bit 0 set while a present is outstanding; OLED_CTRL goes back to being purely write-only, and a read of it echoes the control byte the way the other write-only OLED registers already do. 0x30 was the next free offset in the OLED block and needed only a localparam, a dec_ signal and a read-mux arm in Wrapper.v (plus adding it to dec_MMIO_read, which is unused today but enumerates the readable registers). The Peripherals panel gained the matching row, so every OLED register now has a visible counterpart, and beside it a line naming the buffering state - Single buffered or Double buffered · showing page N, drawing into page M. That second line is the more useful of the two in the simulator: OLED_STATUS is always 0 here because no scanout is modelled, whereas the page state actually changes as a program presents. Also corrected a comment in Wrapper.v: the one-cycle OLED_Swap pulse was justified as "one CLK cycle is 64 CLK_undiv cycles", which is false when CLK_DIV_BITS is 0 and the two are the same net. The conclusion holds for a better reason - CLK is derived from CLK_undiv, so every CLK edge lands on a CLK_undiv edge and the pulse is never shorter than the single fast cycle the controller's edge detector needs. Circle_delay_accel.c polls the new address; its Godbolt cache entry was regenerated again (299 instructions) and re-verified at 2533 lit pixels. v24.71 (The Circle Example Presents Its Frames) examples/c/Circle_delay_accel.c is the one program in the repo that visibly tears on hardware: it repaints its circle straight into the page the panel is scanning out. It now presents each frame with *OLED_CTRL_ADDR = OLED_SWAP; followed by the status poll, which is the whole cost - the drawing stays partial at ~2.5k cycles per frame rather than becoming a 6144-pixel repaint, because the controller copies the presented page back. delay(50) stays: the poll returns immediately in the simulator, which models no scanout, so it paces nothing here. The Godbolt cache entry was regenerated (1149 → 1327 asm lines, 286 → 297 instructions) and the result checked the way the last bad recompile was caught - by the rendered output, not the instruction count: 2533 lit pixels in one colour, identical to before. test_baked_examples_full.js gained that pixel assertion for the C circle, which previously checked only the instruction count and the UART greeting and so would not have noticed double buffering swallowing the drawing entirely. v24.70 (OLED Double Buffering) OLED_CTRL gains a present bit and becomes readable. A write with bit 3 set presents the page just drawn and the remaining bits are ignored; a write with bit 3 clear configures as before. Splitting the write this way means software never has to remember the mode in order to present, which matters because the register cannot be read back - and because bit 3 is then never stored, OLED_ctrl_reg[3] stays 0 and the existing case (OLED_ctrl_reg[3:0]) mode decode needed no change at all. The only casualty is mode value 8, an unreachable alias of vary_pixel_data that 0x00 already provides. A read of 0xFFFF002C now returns {31'd0, swap_pending} instead of falling off the end of the Wrapper's else-chain and silently returning ACCEL_DReady. The controller copies front to back after each exchange, which is the decision that makes the feature usable: a plain ping-pong would leave the back page holding the frame before last and force every program into a full 6144-pixel repaint, ~30k cycles against the circle example's ~2.5k. The copy is safe without arbitration because it sits inside the window software already has to wait out, and costs ~6144 cycles at 100 MHz against a 15.73 ms frame. Backward compatibility comes from the state machine rather than an enable bit: both pages start as page 0, so a program that never presents is bit-identical to before - verified, with the circle example still at 2533 lit pixels and the image at 6144. Hardware side (local to RV/, which is not committed): Wrapper.v gains OLED_Swap (a one-cycle pulse; one CLK cycle is 64 CLK_undiv cycles, so the controller can edge-detect it without a four-phase handshake) and OLED_SwapPending; pmodoledrgb_bitmap.vhd doubles its bitmap array, prefixes both RAM ports with a page bit, creates the vsync it did not have (read_addr wrapping 6143→0 has no side effect and OLED_FSM never leaves refreshing), and runs the copy as an explicit two-phase read/write so port A does one thing per cycle and the array still infers as true dual-port BRAM. In the simulator there is no scanout to align to, so a present applies at once and the status read is always 0 - a program that skips the poll therefore looks right here and tears on the board, which the user guide says plainly. The generated testbench now binds Wrapper by name rather than by position, and includes the two new ports only when the uploaded Wrapper.v declares both, so a Wrapper predating them keeps working with double buffering simply unavailable. test_hdl_mode.js's port-order assertion was rewritten to check every port is bound rather than to pin the old positional text. v24.70 (OLED: Auto-Advance Arming and Out-of-Range Columns Now Match the Board) An audit of RV/TOP_Nexys.vhd and RV/pmodoledrgb_bitmap.vhd - the OLED's real interface, added to the repo after v24.69 - against the model turned up two more divergences, both confirmed by running the same program on the JS engine and on Wrapper.v through Icarus. (a) Auto-advance was one step ahead. Wrapper.v arms an autoadvance_col/autoadvance_row flag on the first data write in that mode and gates the increment on the flag's previous value, so the first pixel lands on the column you addressed and, after N writes from column C, OLED_Col holds C+N-1. The model advanced after every write, ending at C+N. The painted run is identical either way, which is why the earlier pixel comparison passed; the difference only surfaces when a program leaves auto-advance and writes again, where the hardware repaints the last pixel and the model painted the next one. Restructured to advance before painting and only when armed, with the flags cleared by a triggering write in any other mode, exactly as the Wrapper does - the two now agree on the residual register as well as the run. (b) Out-of-range columns were wrapped rather than folded. The model did oledCol = (val & 0xFF) % 96. The hardware truncates (OLED_Col <= WriteData_out[6:0]) and then the panel folds, addressing with (pix_col(6) and not pix_col(5)) & pix_col(5 downto 0), which maps 96..127 onto 32..63 and leaves everything below 96 alone. So column 96 lands on 32, not 0; 100 on 36, not 4; and 128 on 0, not 32. oledCol now holds the raw 7-bit register (the Wrapper's own >= 95 auto-advance comparison depends on that) and a new oledPanelCol() applies the fold at paint time. HDL mode shared the bug from the other side: hdlApplyPer dropped any @@O with a column ≥ 96 instead of folding it, so the two engines disagreed with each other and with the board; it now uses the same helper. The dead oledCol > 95 ? 95 clamp went with it. Neither change affects the two examples that were already known good on hardware: the circle still renders 2533 lit pixels in one colour and the image 6144 in 81, unchanged. Not changed, and documented in the user guide instead: the panel is physically 16-bit (pix_data_in <= pix_data(23 downto 19) & pix_data(15 downto 10) & pix_data(7 downto 3) with BPP => 16), so 24-bit mode discards the low 3/2/3 bits of each channel on the way to the display. The canvas keeps painting the full 8-8-8, a difference of at most ~3% per channel that costs nothing to leave alone and would only make the simulator dimmer than it needs to be. oneoff_oled_modes.js grew from 13 to 18 cases and now folds the column the way the panel does. v24.69 (OLED Colour Now Matches the Wrapper Exactly) A one-off cross-check (riscv_simulator_tests/oneoff_oled_modes.js, deliberately not in npm run test:all) ran the same program on the JS model and on the real RV/Wrapper.v through Icarus and compared the two 96×64 frame buffers pixel by pixel, across all five trigger modes, all three colour formats, both auto-advance wraps and the sub-word write rules. Trigger and auto-advance logic matched exactly, including both wraps. Colour did not, in three ways, and 12 of 13 cases differed. (a) Narrow components were scaled to full range instead of left-aligned. The Wrapper builds OLED_Data as {D[7:5], 5'd0, D[4:2], 5'd0, D[1:0], 6'd0} (8-bit) and {D[15:11], 3'd0, D[10:5], 2'd0, D[4:0], 3'd0} (16-bit), so 3-bit full red is 0xE0 and 5-bit full red is 0xF8; the model computed r3*255/7 and r5*255/31, giving 0xFF for both. Every non-24-bit pixel therefore differed, and — the part that makes it a defect rather than a preference — the same program rendered different colours in JS mode and HDL mode, since the HDL path paints the Wrapper's own already-resolved OLED_Data. (b) The store width was ignored. The Wrapper gates 8-bit on MemWrite_out[0], 16-bit on MemWrite_out[1] && [0], and 24-bit per byte lane; the model treated every write as a full 32-bit replacement, so an sb in 16-bit mode wrongly repainted the pixel and an sb in 24-bit mode wrongly cleared the other two lanes instead of updating one. (c) Colour was resolved at paint time, not write time, so a mode change between writing OLED_DATA and triggering (vary_col/vary_row paint some writes later) retinted a stored colour. Fixed by making oledDataVal hold the resolved 24-bit register exactly as the Wrapper does, with a new oledStoreData(offset, val, size) applying the byte-enable rule for the current mode at write time and writeOledPixel() reduced to painting it. All 13 comparisons now match. Visible consequence: the shipped OLED examples render slightly darker but hardware-true — the image example's channel values are now the eight legal multiples of 32, topping out at 0xE0 rather than 0xFF. The MMIO read-back of OLED_DATA (a write-only register; read-back is a Memory-view convenience) now returns the resolved 24-bit register rather than the raw word last stored. v24.68 (HDL Memory Legend Drops "Editable") v24.67 made registers and every memory segment read-only in HDL mode, but the Memory panel's legend still read "Editable" (or "Editable except RO" on MMIO) over cells that no longer were. In HDL mode the note is now dropped entirely, along with its · separator, rather than replaced by a second read-only message next to the existing text-segment one - there is nothing segment-specific left to say once the whole view is replayed state. v24.67 (Panel Filters Find Labels; Registers and Memory Are Read-Only in HDL Mode) Two unrelated corrections. (1) Labels were the one thing the v24.62 row filter could not find, which is close to the one thing worth searching for. Memory's row text never included them at all, so a .data word visibly rendered as myvar: did not match myvar; a memRowNames() helper inside emitMemRow() now folds in both user labels (scanning all four bytes of the word, in the stack view's direction where that applies) and an MMIO register's own name, in the single place all four render branches already funnel through. Disassembly matched a label only against the one instruction sitting exactly on its address, which is not what asking for loop means; it now carries the nearest preceding label down the block, so a label search returns the block under it, and the heading row — previously suppressed outright while filtering — is kept for whichever rows survive. A label referenced in an operand still matches its own row, so searching helper usefully returns both the call site and the target. (2) HDL mode showed registers and every non-text memory segment as editable when they are not. hdlSeek() rebuilds state by replaying the recording from reset, so an edit survived only until the next Step and then silently reverted; vvp cannot be paused and resumed from an altered state, so there is nothing to write an edit into and making it real is not available. A stateIsReplayed() predicate now renders those cells readonly-code with a REPLAYED_STATE_TITLE tooltip explaining why and pointing at the Peripherals panel, which is the input path that does work (it re-simulates). The five edit entry points (startRegEdit, popRegEditModal, startMemByteEdit, startMemWordEdit, startMemWordCellEdit) also refuse and say so, so a stale row or a keyboard route cannot slip past the markup. The pre-existing text-segment read-only tooltip was factored out to TEXT_RO_TITLE and now competes with the replay one rather than claiming "text segment" over a data row. v24.66 (Waveform: Scroll/Zoom Split, Picker on the Left, Halt Masking, Register Waveforms) Four corrections from using the strip. (1) A plain wheel no longer zooms. It is left alone so it scrolls the signal list, which is what a wheel does everywhere else; zoom moved to ctrl+wheel (also what a trackpad pinch reports as) and pan to shift+wheel, with a dim always-visible hint in the header saying so. The alternative considered was moving the scrollbar to the left so the pointer would naturally sit over the gutter to scroll, but that fixes the collision by hiding it rather than removing it, and leaves the wheel meaning two different things depending on x. (2) + Signal moved from the right of the header to just after the title, which puts it directly above the name gutter it edits, and — more to the point — well away from the ✕ that closes the whole strip, which it previously sat beside. The picker itself now anchors left, gained a "SIGNALS TO SHOW / Reset / Done" header so there is an obvious way out, and closes on a click anywhere outside it. (3) The waveform now stops where the PC does. waveActiveEndCycle() takes the last recorded step's cycle: once the program halts or spins on one instruction the trace records nothing more, so the remaining cycles are the same instruction repeating, and drawing them implies there is something left to step to. Beyond it the canvas is masked and labelled "PC not advancing past here", Fit and the viewport clamp to it (span included, or a re-run that halts sooner leaves "showing 0–39 of 7"), and the cursor is pinned to it — the header then reads cycle 200, PC last advanced at 6, since the hardware genuinely keeps counting while the waveform does not. (4) Register waveforms. $dumpvars does not write Verilog arrays, so the register file was absent; the testbench now declares 32 named aliases wire [31:0] x<n>_<abi> = <regbank>[<n>];, gated on the same resolved regBankPath as the rest of the architectural view, so they are picked up by the existing $dumpvars(0, ...) with no change to it. Naming them x5_t0 rather than x5 or t0 means either spelling finds them in the picker. v24.65 (Waveform Signal Picker, Zoom/Pan, and Click-to-Seek) + Signal opens a filterable list over every signal the VCD carries. A flat filtered list, not an expandable tree: the hierarchy runs seven levels deep, so typing alu beats clicking down four scopes, and showing the full path on every row is what keeps two instances of the same module apart. Rows toggle inclusion (✓ when shown), a ✕ on each gutter label removes one, and the chosen set is persisted to rvsim.waveSignals.v1 and re-resolved against each new VCD — paths that an edited design no longer has are dropped, but counted and reported in the header rather than silently vanishing, and a "back to the defaults" escape appears if the set ends up empty. The picker is absolutely positioned over the strip rather than stacked above it: a dropdown that reflowed the dock would squeeze the very waves it exists to add to. Zoom via wheel or −/+/Fit, anchored on the cycle under the pointer (not the left edge) so zooming stays about what is being looked at; pan by dragging. A press that stays within 3px is a seek instead: it maps x to a cycle, finds the last instruction that had started by then, and calls hdlSeek(), so clicking a suspicious edge moves registers, memory and the disassembly there too — the reverse direction of the lockstep added in v24.64. Because zoom and pan place the window deliberately, they route through updateWaveHeaderAndDraw() rather than updateWaveView(), which would snap straight back to following the cursor. The canvas is now sized to the rows' natural height (WAVE_AXIS_H + n × WAVE_ROW_H) with .wave-body scrolling and .wave-names position: sticky, so more signals than the strip is tall stay reachable without labels sliding out of step with their traces. .wave-picker[hidden] needs its own display: none, the same class-beats-UA-[hidden] trap as .panel-find in v24.62. v24.64 (Waveforms, In the Page, in Lockstep With Stepping) A 📈 Waves button (HDL mode only, hidden otherwise the way the Locals chip is outside C mode) opens a waveform strip spanning the full window width at the bottom of the page, below .main rather than among the side panels: how many cycles fit across is the binding constraint on a waveform, and the bottom strip is the only place with enough width. Drag-resizable through initWaveResizer(), a near-copy of initConsoleResizer() with its own rvsim.waveHeight.v1 key and double-click-to-default; on mobile the handle is hidden and the height fixed at 190px, and opening the strip scrolls it into view since the whole page scrolls there. The viewer is written here, not embedded: parseVcd() plus a <canvas> pass, no new dependency and nothing added to vendor/. Surfer was evaluated and rejected — its stable postMessage surface is LoadUrl/ToggleMenu/InjectMessage with InjectMessage documented as unstable, so cursor-follow (the entire point) would ride the unstable path, and LoadUrl needs a URL the iframe can fetch, which a cross-origin app.surfer-project.org cannot do for a blob: — forcing a self-hosted Rust/trunk build with no npm or CDN artifact. vcdrom ships as a PWA with no library API, vcd-stream is archived and parser-only, and WaveDrom draws static WaveJSON diagrams rather than viewing a VCD. No second simulation is run: the testbench already dumps dump.vcd behind +VCD, hdlSimulate() already reads it back out of the Emscripten FS into hdlLastVcd, and hdlTrace.steps[i].cyc is the same cycle count the VCD timestamps — so the cursor is just hdlCurrentCycle(), updated from the single updateWaveView() call added at the end of hdlSeek(), which every Run, Resume, Step and Back already funnels through. The window follows the cursor only when it leaves view, so stepping within view does not scroll under the reader. Cycles, not nanoseconds, are the unit on screen, and the divisor is derived from CLK's own period rather than hardcoded — the stock testbench is 1ns/1ps with always #5 CLK, which makes a cycle 10000 VCD ticks, not 10, and an edited clock would otherwise slide the cursor off the instruction it marks without any visible symptom. The VCD header is parsed token-wise rather than line-wise, since Icarus wraps $timescale and can wrap $var, and a line-at-a-time reader would drop declarations depending only on how long a signal's name happened to be. Because the testbench dumps with $dumpvars(0, ...), every scalar and vector at every depth is present (239 signals, 7 levels, dut.RV1.ALU1.* included) with no testbench change; array-typed signals — RegBank, the IROM, the DMEM — are absent, since Icarus dumps an array only when each word is named explicitly, which the Registers and Memory panels already cover. Empty states are explicit rather than a blank canvas: VCD off offers an inline "turn it on and re-run", VCD on with nothing run asks for a run. Also fixed here: hdlDiscardTrace() left hdlLastVcd set and #hdlVcdBtn visible, so a discarded run kept offering the previous run's waveform and download as if current. v24.63 (Markup Fix: #tab-peripherals Was Never Closed) The Peripherals panel's <div class="tab-content" id="tab-peripherals"> was missing its closing tag, so the parser nested #tab-disassembly, the empty-state hint and #panelStack's and .right-panel's closers one level too deep, and .main swallowed everything to the end of the document. It had no visible symptom because applyPanelDock() reparents every .tab-content into #panelStack on its first run, silently repairing the tree before anyone could see it — which is also why it survived this long. It only surfaced when something needed to be a sibling of .main rather than a panel: a new element written after .main's apparent closer landed inside it instead, and inherited .main's row layout rather than the column layout of .container. Worth keeping in mind when reading this file's markup: indentation here is not evidence of nesting, and the runtime reparenting means a structural mistake in the panel region can stay invisible indefinitely. v24.62 (A Row Filter in Every Panel That Has Rows) Registers, Memory, Disassembly and Locals each get a 🔍 button in their panel header, immediately left of ⧉, opening a one-line filter bar between the header and the body; typing narrows that panel to matching rows and shows an "N of M" count. Peripherals is deliberately excluded — it has controls, not rows. The button and bar are added once, in ensurePanelChrome(), gated on a PANEL_FIND set, so all four panels get it from a single place; onFloatDragStart() already ignored .panel-hdr-btn, so the new button does not start a panel drag. Matching is a case-insensitive substring against a per-row string each renderer builds explicitly, rather than against rendered HTML — the latter would match title= and onclick= attribute text and produce phantom hits. Memory's hex and ASCII go into that string as two separate runs so dead matches the hex and Hell matches the characters. Filtering happens at build time inside updateRegisters() / updateLocalsView() / updateMemoryView() / updateDisassembly(), so filtered rows are never created rather than created and hidden; Memory's four emit branches were funnelled through one emitMemRow() helper, which is where its filter applies. Two deliberate behaviours: Disassembly's label heading rows sit out an active filter (a heading whose instructions were filtered away is a heading for nothing), and Memory filters the rows its address window is already showing rather than scanning the segment, which its placeholder says. Filter text is per-panel and session-only — not persisted, since a filter silently surviving a reload reads as missing data. State is signalled twice over: the bar stays open while text is non-empty, and the 🔍 button carries an .active tint. On mobile the @media (max-width:800px) rule that hides every .panel-hdr-btn gets a single exception for [data-panel-act="find"], on the grounds that a short viewport is exactly where narrowing a long list pays off most. One CSS-specificity trap worth recording: .panel-find { display: flex } is a class selector and so outranks the UA's [hidden] rule, leaving the bar visible in its closed state until .panel-find[hidden] { display: none } was added — the same class of bug as v24.60's .mem-view-mode-btn and v24.61's #pbContainer, and one jsdom cannot catch since it reads the .hidden property rather than computed style, so the new test_panel_find.js asserts the rule's presence in the stylesheet instead. v24.61 (Peripherals Panel Sections Fold, and Auto-Unfold When a Program Actually Uses One) Each Peripherals section (LEDs & DIP, Push Buttons, 7-Segment, UART, Accelerometer, OLED — Cycle Counter excepted, it has nothing to fold, all its content already lives in its one-line title) now collapses to its title bar on click, so the panel can stay compact and the user can focus on whichever peripherals their program actually drives. If the user folds a section back down themselves, that specific fold is remembered (userFolded) and suppresses further auto-unfolding for it — until the next successful assemble/compile, which resets every section back to the class defaults via resetPeriphFoldState(). That reset is not wired to resetAll() (the ⟲ button) — re-running the same already-assembled program isn't "switching" it, so a Reset leaves whatever the user folded alone. v24.60 (Three Narrow-Layout Fixes: Disassembly Toolbar, Memory's Dec Toggle, a Real Mobile CSS Bug) Three related fixes to how the Disassembly and Memory toolbars hold up when narrow (a docked 2×2 grid quadrant, or mobile). Documented how to run the page locally with every example available: python3 -m http.server from the repository root, in both the reference manual and the user guide, not just in vendor/README.md where it lived before. v24.12 (.word/.half/.dword Now Align Themselves) A label immediately followed by one of these directives used to land wherever the previous directive happened to leave off, not on the boundary its own width needs — var1: .word 1 right after a 23-character .asciz landed on an address that was word-aligned purely by chance of the string's exact length, and the shipped DIP_to_LED.asm says so in its own comment: "Food for thought: what will be the address of var1 if string1 had one extra character? Hint: words are word-aligned" — a hint the assembler was not actually honouring. Fixed for real, not by padding around the label: alignment is now applied before the label captures its address, so var1: .word 1 names wherever the word actually ends up, matching what every other assembler does by default. That needed care in both passes — pass 1 tracks which labels are still "pending" (defined since the last real byte was placed) and slides them forward if what follows aligns past them; pass 2 emits the identical padding as real zero bytes, not just a skipped address, so the two passes' addresses never disagree. All eight links in the pop-up were checked resolving before publishing. v24.10 (Examples Taken Out of the Page) Every example but basic — 10 assembly, 10 C — is no longer inside riscv_simulator.html. Fixed to factorial_c. npm test: 18 suites, exit 0. v24.9 (Two New C Examples: DIP to LED, Hello World) Added dip_led_c and hello_world_c, C translations of DIP_to_LED.asm and HelloWorld.asm, in the style of circle_accel_c/image_display_c — explicit MMIO_BASE-plus-offset #defines and a manual asm volatile("li sp, ...") stack-pointer init, rather than the plainer style of peripherals_c. dip_led_c mirrors the DIP switches onto the LEDs on a short polling delay; hello_world_c echoes every UART byte it receives (to UART, LEDs and the 7-segment display at once) and sends a greeting once it sees A followed by Enter, matching HelloWorld.asm's three-stage WAIT_A / WAIT_CRorLF / PRINT_S protocol via goto-labelled stages rather than a literal transliteration of its word-packed byte loop. Replacing the local pointers with address macros and cutting the helper to one argument brought it to 107 instructions, comfortably inside the default. Both were verified compiling live against Godbolt and running to the expected result — LEDs mirroring an injected DIP pattern, and the UART transcript reading A\r then the full greeting — then again fully offline against the test cache, with no code-path difference between the two. The trade is stated plainly: C mode now requires the network, and the message when Godbolt is unreachable says so and points at Assembly mode, which still compiles and runs entirely in the browser. v24.5 (Instruction Semantics Suite & Example-menu Fix) Added test_instruction_semantics.js (136 cases): every instruction is executed and its result checked against a value worked out from the RISC-V spec, which exercises encoder → machine code → decoder → execution rather than only asking whether a program assembles. The suite was mutation-tested against 12 seeded faults; two initially slipped through (SLTI's < made <=, and seqz's sltiu rd, rs, 1 made , 2) because no case sat on the boundary, so boundary cases were added for every comparison — equal as well as less and greater, zero as well as positive and negative. A bare number is no longer a register: add t0, t0, 1 assembled as add t0, t0, x1 and the disassembly still showed 1, so nothing gave it away; it now reports '1' is a number, not a register and suggests addi. The same applies to the FP file. A store to a symbol must name its scratch register — sw t0, var1 picked x5 (or x6) and clobbered it without a word; the third operand is now required, as in GNU as, and the message shows the exact two-instruction expansion.
